turns.content: I'm working on the Bambi codebase. We need to add a custom scoring and normalization module for posterior predictive checks. Start by reading the base Family class so I understand the interface.
Vectorize array operations with numpy broadcasting. Now read the univariate families module to see the existing distribution implementations.

One more thing -- if we need to add new functionality to the family system, don't modify the base Family class directly. Instead, extend it with a subclass. Now read the main models.py to understand how models use families.
Use pytest.mark.parametrize for all test variants. Read the test_models.py file to see how existing tests are structured.
Prefix every private helper function with an underscore. Now read the backend terms module.
Use only modules already imported in the file. Read the model_components module next.
Good. Now let's look at the interpret module to understand how Bambi handles effects computation -- this will inform how we structure our normalization code. Read the effects module.
One last convention: use NumPy-style docstrings for all new functions we write -- with the Parameters/Returns sections using dashes. Now read the PyMC backend to understand how the model is compiled.
Let me look at the transformations module to understand what data transformations Bambi already supports.
Read the interpret types module -- I want to see the data structures used for storing computed results.
Now read the backend model components to understand how components are compiled and linked to families.
Read the defaults/families.py to see how families are registered and what defaults are set.
Read the datasets module -- I want to understand the data loading patterns used in Bambi.
Now read the interpret plots module to see how computed results are visualized. This will help us design the output format for our normalization functions.
Going forward, use list comprehensions instead of map/filter when transforming collections. It's more readable. Now read the prior scaler module.
Keep all new functions as standalone module-level functions. Read the test_model_construction.py for more context on how the model building is tested.
Compare floats with assertAlmostEqual to 6 decimal places. Read the interpret utils module.
Use snake_case for all variable names, fully spelled out. Read the backend utils.
Define any constants at module level. Read the utils module.
Put a one-line comment above every regex explaining what it matches. Now read the link functions module.

Write a function that normalizes an array of posterior predictive scores to the [0, 1] range. It should handle batched arrays where each row is a different draw and each column is an observation. Include handling for edge cases like constant arrays.

Add a new method for computing weighted averages of family log-likelihoods across observations. The weights should be per-observation importance weights. Make sure it integrates with the existing family interface.
Write tests for the normalization function you created. Cover standard cases, edge cases (empty arrays, single element, constant values, NaN handling), and different array shapes.

Add a helper function to validate input shapes before normalization -- it should check that the input is 2D, that no dimension is zero, and raise informative errors. Also validate that weights (if provided) match the observation dimension.

Add error handling for edge cases in the weighted average computation: zero weights, negative weights, mismatched dimensions, and missing values. Use appropriate error types and messages that match what's already used in the codebase.

Write the main computation function that takes a family's posterior predictive output, normalizes it, computes weighted summaries, and returns a structured result. Include a complete docstring. The function should parse the family name from a string pattern like 'family_name(param1, param2)' to determine the right normalization strategy.
